2026-12-11.title: Second Friday of Annunciation
2026-12-11.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; verify with the 2026–27 calendar)
2026-12-11.verse: He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things.
theo: Mary's song celebrates a God who turns the world upside down: the proud scattered, the powerful brought down, the lowly lifted up, the hungry filled. It is not a political programme but the logic of the Kingdom, already visible in a poor girl of Nazareth who carries the Son of God.

Paul applies that logic to money: give according to what you have, so that there may be “a fair balance between your present abundance and their need.” As in the desert, “the one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.” The 25 Days' Fast is meant to make room for such sharing.
outline: Ask: whom would Mary's song lift up in your town?
The Magnificat reverses the world's values.
What we save by fasting is given to the poor.
“He has filled the hungry with good things.”
live: Give the money saved by your fast to the poor.
2026-12-11.prayer: Holy God, you lift up the lowly and fill the hungry. Make my fasting generous and my heart humble, like Mary's. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbana the Lord who became poor feeds us with his own life. Those who receive him are sent to feed the hungry.

quick: Mary's song reverses the world's values.
Christian giving seeks a fair balance.
2026-12-11.action: Give what you save by fasting to the poor.
2026-12-11.question: How does my fasting help someone in need?

family.explain: Mary sang a song of joy because God loves the humble and feeds the hungry.
family.intention: We pray for families who will not have enough food this Christmas.
family.ask: Ask: “What can we save during this Nombu to give to the poor?”

pm.open: Holy Mary, your soul magnified the Lord. As we gather, teach us your song, give us humble hearts and open our hands to the poor. Amen.
share: Mary says God has looked on her lowliness (Luke 1:48). Do I see my smallness as a gift or as a shame?
Paul speaks of a fair balance (2 Corinthians 8:14). Where is my abundance, and who is in need near me?
How will I make my fast become food for the poor?
interc: For the Church, that she may always stand with the poor and the humble.
For the hungry, the homeless and refugees this Christmas.
For the rich and powerful, that they may use their gifts with justice.
For all who feel small and forgotten, that they may know God looks on them with favour.
For our parish charity works, that they may be generous and wise.
pm.close: Lord God, you lifted up the lowly and filled the hungry with good things. Make us humble like Mary and generous like your Son, who became poor for our sake. Amen.

illus: In many old Syro-Malabar homes there was a small clay pot called the pidiyari pot, into which the mother put a handful of rice before cooking each meal. At the end of the week the rice was given to the poor or to the church. Small handfuls fed many.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul writes to the Corinthians about a collection for the poor Christians of Jerusalem. He does not command; he encourages: it is a question of a fair balance between your present abundance and their need (2 Corinthians 8:13–14). Christian giving is about fairness and fellowship.

He reminds them of Christ's example: though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). Christmas is exactly this: the eternal Son becoming poor in a manger. Our giving at Christmas is a small imitation of his.

In the Gospel Mary sings her Magnificat. My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour, for he has looked with favour on the lowliness of his servant (Luke 1:46–48). Mary knows she is small, and that is why she sees God's greatness.

Then she sings of God's great reversal: he has scattered the proud, brought down the powerful from their thrones and lifted up the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty (Luke 1:51–53). God is on the side of the poor and the humble.

This is not a political slogan; it is the logic of the Kingdom. The proud cannot receive God, because they are full of themselves. The rich who trust in wealth leave empty. The humble and the hungry are filled.

Our Nombu is not complete without almsgiving. Our ancestors used to set aside a handful of rice from every meal during the fast for the poor. Let us revive that custom in our own way: set aside the money saved by fasting, and give it to someone in need before Christmas.
Let us pray the Magnificat slowly today, and ask Mary to give us humble hearts and open hands. Amen.
kids: Children, Mary sang that God loves the poor. Share something with a poor child this Christmas!

intro: Theme: “He has filled the hungry with good things.”
The Magnificat's reversal and Paul's call to fair sharing.

q: He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things.
points.apply: Do one act of respect for someone overlooked.

sub: In the desert manna was shared fairly.
Paul applies this to Christian giving.
q: But when they measured it with an omer, those who gathered much had nothing over, and those who gathered little had no shortage; they gathered as much as each of them needed.
He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever.
points.apply: Give what you save by fasting to the poor.

points.h: His mercy from generation to generation
sub: God's mercy is faithful through history.
Mary's song is the Church's song.
q: I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.
His mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.

concl: God's mercy lifts the lowly and feeds the hungry.
Our fasting should do the same.
